Senanque
say-NAHNK
n. (a Cistercian abbey in a fold of the Vaucluse hills in Provence, founded 1148 and still a monastic community)
From Provençal, probably from a root meaning a dry or sandy valley; the abbey takes its name from the narrow combe it fills.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Sénanque was founded in 1148 in a steep dry combe of the Vaucluse, a daughter of Mazan, and is the only one of the three Provencal sisters still occupied by a monastic community, having been reoccupied in the twentieth century. It is the most photographed abbey in France because of the lavender field in front of it, and that accident of popularity is worth a word, since the flowers in the photograph last six weeks and the building has lasted nine hundred years — while Scripture insists that neither is the enduring thing. “All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field” (Isa 40:6) and “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) set the proportion exactly. Christ draws the other lesson from the same kind of field: “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin” (Mat 6:28) and “That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these” (Mat 6:29). A Cistercian house in a flowering valley was a good place to learn both, and it is not clear that its visitors do.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines flower as the delicate and gaily colored leaves or petals of a plant, and figuratively the prime or best part; valley as a hollow or low tract of land between hills; and fade as to lose color, to wither, to decay.

expand to see more

FLOWER, n. In botany, that part of a plant which contains the organs of generation; also, the delicate and gaily colored leaves or petals; figuratively, the prime, the choicest part.

VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.

FADE, v.i. To lose color; to lose freshness; to wither, as a plant; to decline; to perish gradually.

LILY, n. A genus of plants of many species, bearing beautiful flowers.

WITHER, v.i. To fade; to lose its native freshness; to become sapless; to dry.

Key Scripture

Isa 40:6 — "The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field:"

Isa 40:8 — "The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever."

Mat 6:28 — "And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:"

Mat 6:29 — "And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these."

Modern Corruption

A Provencal house of 1148 in a dry combe, still occupied: the most photographed abbey in France, and a good place to learn that neither flower nor masonry endures.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Isaiah states in the same breath as the flower. “but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) is the only durable thing named in the passage, and a tourist industry built on a six-week bloom in front of a nine-century wall illustrates the point rather than teaching it.

The live misuse is aesthetic Christianity: the abbey as atmosphere, the lavender as mood, monasticism admired as a style by people who would reject every proposition it was built on. Christ's own use of a flowering field is moral and not decorative — “And why take ye thought for raiment?” (Mat 6:28) — and he draws from it a command about anxiety, not a photograph.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsits (H6731), a flower; Hebrew chatsir (H2682), grass; Greek anthos (G438), a flower; Greek krinon (G2918), a lily; Hebrew dabar (H1697), a word.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsits (H6731) — a blossom or flower; “as the flower of the field” (Isa 40:6).

Hebrew chatsir (H2682) — grass, herbage; “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth” (Isa 40:8).

Greek krinon (G2918) — a lily; “Consider the lilies of the field” (Mat 6:28).

Greek anthos (G438) — a flower; Peter quotes Isaiah with this word of all human glory.

Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter; the one thing in the passage that stands.

Usage

"“All flesh is grass” (Isa 40:6) — the measure of every beautiful thing, abbeys included."

"“even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these” (Mat 6:29) — the field above the palace."

"“the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) — the only durable item on the list."
